query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of lattice strain through deposition on a substrate with a mismatched lattice parameter alters the magnetostructural transition dynamics, leading to reduced hysteresis and improved magnetocaloric response in as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys.
generation.intervention: Introducing a controlled amount of lattice strain through deposition on a substrate with a mismatched lattice parameter
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced hysteresis and improved magnetocaloric response
generation.baseline: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys without lattice strain
generation.boundary: Within the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements and retaining mechanical stability
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the effect of lattice strain on the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis is uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys on substrates with varying lattice parameters and measure the resulting magnetocaloric response and hysteresis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant change in magnetocaloric response or hysteresis is observed with varying lattice strain, the hypothesis is falsified

Dislocation slip twins were the main deformation mechanism of the AlCrFeCuNi high-entropy alloy. Due to severe lattice distortion and high local strain, the CoNiFeAlCu alloy induced a phase transition from FCC to BCC. The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment. A wide spectrum of magnetic properties has been reported ranging from soft to semi-soft magnetic behavior in their coercivity. Among these alloys, the most studied single-phase FCC Cantor alloy exhibited multiple magnetic transitions from disordered paramagnetic phase to spin glass and subsequently to an ordered ferromagnetic state at low temperatures. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has focused on their unique properties, such as their ability to exhibit a single-phase solid solution, high strength, and high thermal stability. Recent studies have explored the effects of non-equiatomic compositions and the introduction of lattice strain on the properties of these alloys. The trend suggests that the introduction of lattice strain can lead to improved mechanical properties and a more stable microstructure.
decision.unsolved: The governing mechanism of the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys remains unknown. The effects of lattice strain and non-equiatomic compositions on the magnetocaloric properties of these alloys are not well understood.
decision.lever: introducing a controlled amount of lattice strain through deposition on a substrate with a mismatched lattice parameter
decision.why: This approach would allow for the systematic study of the effects of lattice strain on the magnetocaloric properties of the alloy, and could provide insight into the governing mechanism of the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis. The introduction of lattice strain has been shown to improve mechanical properties in other high-entropy alloys, and may have a similar effect on the magnetocaloric properties.
